clue.text: Complaint nieces regularly raised, discussing historic Greece

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means the picked letters are read from bottom to top
taking every other letter of nieces, here the even ones
discussing means talking about, so the next piece is heard rather than seen

parts.note: Attica, the ancient region around Athens

explanation.surface: An aunt's nieces keep bringing up classical Greece in conversation and it gets on her nerves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes I, C, S from nieces and 'raised' turns them to SCI; 'discussing' signals that ATTICA is said aloud, giving the spelling ATICA.
explanation.definitionFit: Sciatica is a painful nerve condition in the lower back and leg, an ailment or medical complaint.

clue.text: Agent's final line of action to enrich financial rate for sportsman

indicators.note: enriching something puts extra material inside it, so these letters go within the rate

parts.note: AER is the annual equivalent rate quoted on UK savings accounts

indicators.note: final picks the last letter of the word agent

parts.note: a tack is a course or approach, as in changing tack

explanation.surface: A bank agent plans a final push to boost the interest rate.
explanation.walkthrough: AER, the annual equivalent rate on British savings, is less familiar outside the UK.
explanation.definitionFit: An attacker is a forward player in team sports, so an example of a sportsman.

clue.text: Positive hospital X-ray developed covering new part of body

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hospital on road signs

indicators.note: covering means the rearranged letters sit around the next piece
developed suggests something worked into a new form, so the letters of X-ray are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, its four letters

explanation.surface: A hospital X-ray comes back positive, revealing something in a newly examined part of the body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'developed' rearranges XRAY to ARYX, and 'covering' wraps that round N to give ARYNX.
explanation.definitionFit: The pharynx is the throat cavity behind the nose and mouth, an anatomical part of the body.

clue.text: Wounds boosted by firm plaster

indicators.note: in a down clue, boosted means pushed upward, so the word is read from the bottom up

parts.note: cuts are wounds, used here as a noun
CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A first-aider finds that wounds heal better thanks to a sturdy plaster from a reputable company.
explanation.definitionFit: Stucco is a fine plaster used for coating walls and decorative mouldings.

clue.text: Tripe starts to kick in, giving nasty smell on mum

indicators.note: starts to takes the opening letter of each of the following two words

parts.note: BO is body odour
mum, as in keep mum, means silence, which is sh

explanation.surface: Tripe begins to take effect, giving off a horrid smell over mother's kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: Kibosh is old slang for nonsense or rubbish, the same sense as tripe meaning worthless talk.

clue.text: Flick twig with a crook

parts.note: to twig is to understand, to catch on, read as an infinitive
a crook is a criminal, such as a robber

explanation.surface: Someone flicks a twig while holding a shepherd's crook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flick' is slang for a film: this is the 1955 Hitchcock thriller with Cary Grant and Grace Kelly.
explanation.definitionFit: A flick is informal for a movie, and this is the title of a Hitchcock film.

clue.text: Designer name written in concrete near building

indicators.note: written in means the abbreviation is placed inside the rearranged letters
building suggests construction, so the letters are put together in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A designer's name is inscribed in the concrete beside a new building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'building' rearranges CONCRETE NEAR, and 'written in' puts N among those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Terence Conran was a British designer and founder of the Habitat furniture stores.

clue.text: Lottery pay leads to party on boat northwards

parts.note: to foot a bill is to pay it
a ball is a formal dancing party

indicators.note: in a down clue, northwards means the word is read from the bottom up

parts.note: a sloop is a single-masted sailing boat

explanation.surface: Lottery winnings fund a party on a boat heading north.
explanation.walkthrough: The football pools were a British betting game predicting match results, a long-running weekly gamble before the National Lottery.
explanation.definitionFit: The football pools are a form of gambling on match results, a kind of lottery with prize money.

clue.text: Character in Marathon, around runner's perimeter area, slips

indicators.note: around means the Greek letter surrounds the following pieces

parts.note: Marathon is in Greece, so its character is a Greek letter, eta

indicators.note: perimeter takes only the outside letters of the word runner

explanation.surface: A competitor in the marathon slips while running around the perimeter of the course.
explanation.definitionFit: Errata are mistakes in printing or writing, little slips listed for correction.

clue.text: Expect record by Yoko and John, ultimately, to go beyond £1000

indicators.note: going beyond means coming after, so these letters follow the thousand

parts.note: K stands for a thousand, as in a grand
on can mean by or next to, as in a house on the river

indicators.note: ultimately takes the last letter of each named person

explanation.surface: A Yoko Ono and John Lennon record is predicted to sell for over a thousand pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: To reckon on something is to count on it happening, a phrasal synonym for anticipate.

clue.text: Opener of canal line to turn on waterworks

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter

parts.note: RY is the abbreviation for railway, a line

explanation.surface: The first lock on a canal is opened to set the water flowing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn on the waterworks' is a jokey idiom for starting to weep, though the surface reads as plumbing.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn on the waterworks is to start shedding tears, which is to weep.

clue.text: Allowed to purchase books (mid-range of prices) with payment deferred

indicators.note: purchase can mean a grip or hold, so the outer piece holds the others inside

parts.note: OK means permitted, all right
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

indicators.note: the mid-range of a word is its central letters

explanation.surface: A shopper is permitted to buy books in the middle price band and pay later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'purchase' looks like buying but here means taking hold, so OK holds NT and IC.
explanation.definitionFit: Buying on tick is informal British for buying on credit, settling the bill later.

clue.text: One confused by pressure cooker that's electronic?

definitions.text: One confused by pressure cooker that's electronic?

indicators.note: confused shows the letters of one are jumbled

parts.note: P is the symbol for pressure in physics
a hob is the cooking surface of a stove
E is short for electronic, as in e-mail

explanation.surface: Someone baffled by a newfangled electronic pressure cooker.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a person bewildered by modern gadgets fears the new.
explanation.definitionFit: A neophobe has an aversion to novelty, so is the kind of person baffled by unfamiliar gadgetry.

clue.text: F1 help? Good advice turned up

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the word is read from the bottom up

parts.note: a tip is a helpful piece of advice

explanation.surface: Wondering whether some sound advice will help a Formula One team.
explanation.definitionFit: In Formula One racing the pit is where cars stop for tyres and repairs, a place of assistance.

clue.text: Opposing sides in league game keep playing here in France

indicators.note: the sides of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: taken as written; only its ends are used

indicators.note: the game animal keeps the opposing letter in play, holding it inside

parts.note: a hare is a game animal, hunted for sport
V is versus, the opposing of two teams

explanation.surface: Rival teams in a league match play on in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' is not a match but hunted wildlife, HARE, which holds V for versus.
explanation.definitionFit: Le Havre is a port city in Normandy, a place in France.

clue.text: Contend events like tennis, removing tops initially

indicators.note: remove the top letter of each word and take what is then first, its second letter

explanation.surface: Arguing about sporting events such as tennis, shedding tops at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: To vie is to compete or strive against rivals, which is what contend means.

clue.text: Perhaps a real eccentric receives nervous response

indicators.note: receives means the rearranged letters take in the next piece
eccentric means odd or off-centre, so the letters of real are rearranged

parts.note: a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: A genuinely odd person reacts with a twitch of nerves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' looks like a throwaway word, but it is the definition: the word a is an indefinite article.
explanation.definitionFit: The word a is the indefinite article in grammar, an example of this part of speech.

clue.text: Political activists argued vehemently in street

indicators.note: vehemently suggests violent agitation, so the letters of argued are shaken up

parts.note: RD is the abbreviation for road, a street

explanation.surface: Activists had a fierce argument out on the street.
explanation.definitionFit: The Red Guards were Mao's student militants in China's Cultural Revolution, political activists.

clue.text: Bono perhaps represents royalty in republic

indicators.note: in places these pieces inside the country name

parts.note: Iran is an Islamic republic
is can mean represents, as in this symbol is danger
HM is His or Her Majesty

explanation.surface: Bono stands for royalty in a republic.
explanation.walkthrough: Bono, U2's singer, was born in Dublin.
explanation.definitionFit: Bono is a Dubliner, so an example of a man from Ireland.

clue.text: Revolutionary clip by broadcasters

parts.note: a clip is a brisk pace, as is a trot
Sky is a British TV broadcaster

explanation.surface: A rebel's film clip is picked up by broadcasting companies.
explanation.definitionFit: Leon Trotsky was a leader of the Russian Revolution, a Bolshevik insurgent.

clue.text: Diet of rum — in other words, heavenly

indicators.note: rum means odd or strange, so the letters of diet of are jumbled

parts.note: or introduces an alternative phrasing, as in other words does

explanation.surface: Living on rum, put another way, is paradise.
explanation.definitionFit: Something described as to die for is wonderful or divine, the informal sense of heavenly.

clue.text: Currently successful position of schoolmaster?

definitions.meaning: playing or performing well at present
a teacher's place is in a class, or form, at school

explanation.definitionFit: Being on good form means performing well, and a teacher stands among a class, a school form.

clue.text: Ensign attached to vessel

parts.note: an ensign is a flag flown on a ship
on can mean fastened to, as with a button on a coat

explanation.surface: A naval flag tied to a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessel' suggests a ship after 'Ensign', but it is a container for drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A flagon is a large bottle or jug for wine or cider, a drinking vessel.

clue.text: Over-emotional teetotal drinks one unit (softly, softly)

indicators.note: drinks means takes in, so the outer word swallows the inner letters

parts.note: dry means abstaining from alcohol
I is the Roman numeral for one, a single unit
P is piano, softly in music, so twice gives PP

explanation.surface: A teetotaller downs a single unit very quietly.
explanation.definitionFit: Drippy is informal for soppy or weakly sentimental, given to excessive feeling.

clue.text: What starts old Meldrew grumbling 'I don't believe it'?

indicators.note: starts takes the opening letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: What triggers grumpy old Victor Meldrew's famous catchphrase?
explanation.walkthrough: Victor Meldrew is the grouchy pensioner of the British sitcom One Foot in the Grave, whose catchphrase was 'I don't believe it!'.
explanation.definitionFit: The text abbreviation is an exclamation of disbelief or astonishment, a modern equivalent of his cry.

clue.text: Fringe screened by tense film-maker

indicators.note: screened by means hidden behind, so the other word wraps around these letters

parts.note: taut means tense or tightly drawn
a ruff is a frilled collar or fringe of feathers

explanation.surface: A fringe festival show is screened by a nervous director.
explanation.definitionFit: François Truffaut was a French New Wave director, a celebrated maker of movies.

clue.text: Release unionist husband trapped in corner

indicators.note: trapped in means the letter is enclosed by the next word

parts.note: a nook is a corner or recess

explanation.surface: A husband cornered by a trade unionist is freed.
explanation.definitionFit: To unhook is to unfasten or set free from a hook or clasp, which is to release.

clue.text: People occupied in repairing barn doors, here in rural England

indicators.note: occupied in means the people sit within the rearranged letters
repairing suggests putting things back together, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: folk means people

explanation.surface: Country folk busy mending barn doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'here' points to a place, not a person busy at the barn. The Norfolk Broads are a network of rivers and lakes in eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norfolk Broads are a waterland area of eastern England, a rural region of the country.
